chapter_title: Nine Gold Medals (The World of Limitless Possibilities)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 5 periods = 250 minutes
Total: 5 periods · 4h 10min

periods.activity_title: Entering the Poem — Reading, Gist, and Imagery

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.156): paired discussion — Olympics, Special Olympics, Paralympics differences
Check Your Understanding (p.159–160): match eight gist descriptions to the correct stanzas

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads a brief paired exchange on the three categories of international games — Olympics, Special Olympics, and Paralympics. Students share what they already know; teacher draws out the key distinction that Special Olympics is designed for athletes with intellectual disabilities.

Unhurried read-aloud of all eight stanzas of 'Nine Gold Medals' (p.156–158), teacher reading with expression while students follow. Pauses after stanza 4 and stanza 6 to let the narrative turn sink in; students track the emotional arc silently.

Students work in pairs to match the eight gist descriptions to the correct stanzas from Check Your Understanding (p.159–160). Pairs compare answers with neighbours before whole-class verification; teacher clarifies the stanza-by-stanza narrative sequence.

Quick paired exchange: students list words they associate with 'empathy' from the poem's imagery and share two contributions each with the class. Teacher notes responses on the board to build a shared word-bank around the poem's central theme.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's narrative arc hinges on a single turn — the eight runners stopping to help the fallen athlete — so drawing attention to the stanza-by-stanza sequence in the gist-matching task anchors that moment precisely. Students may conflate 'empathy' with 'sympathy'; the word-bank activity at the close surfaces those distinctions without formal instruction. The tasks on matching 'empathy', 'sympathy', and 'compassion' to sentences (p.156) have not been anchored here and may be set as a reflective self-study after students have read the poem.

periods.activity_title: Appreciating Craft — Imagery, Tone, and Poetic Devices

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Appreciation (p.160): identify alliteration, visual and auditory imagery; analyse how imagery appeals and how tone shifts

homework.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.159): match five words/phrases to their contextual meanings from the poem

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads stanzas 4–6 aloud again with students following, drawing attention to sound patterns. Students are asked to listen for repeated consonant sounds and any words that create a picture or make a sound in the mind.

Students work through the Reading for Appreciation questions (p.160) individually, then compare with a partner: identifying two examples of alliteration, three of visual imagery, one of auditory imagery, and noting how each device contributes to the poem's emotional texture. Teacher circulates, prompting students to cite the exact line or phrase.

Whole-class discussion on the tone questions: how the tone shifts from anticipatory excitement through anguish to warm affirmation, what the overall mood is, and what message the poem conveys. Teacher draws a simple three-phase tone arc on the board as students contribute.

Students write two sentences independently: one naming a device they found most powerful and explaining why. Teacher takes two or three responses to read aloud, affirming the variety of valid choices — this consolidates the analytical habit of naming a device and explaining its effect.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem in full during the earlier sitting, students bring a narrative understanding to the craft analysis here; the task now demands naming devices and explaining their effect, not just finding them. A common difficulty is treating alliteration as any repeated sound rather than repeated initial consonants — direct attention to 'stumbled and staggered' as the clearest example. The contextual word-matching task (p.159) is set as homework to consolidate unfamiliar vocabulary before the extract-based work in the following unit.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.161): Extract 2 — five questions on the final stanza: emotion, gold medals rationale, fill-in, standing ovation MCQ, last-line explanation
Vocabulary in Context (p.162): identify two adjective–noun collocations from the poem besides 'standing ovation'

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Extract 2 — the final stanza — aloud (p.161), then invites students to read it silently one more time. Students are told they will analyse this stanza closely, attending to what the poet chooses to show rather than tell.

Students answer all five Critical Reflection questions on Extract 2 (p.161) individually: how the nine contestants felt at the finish line, why all nine received gold medals, completing the 'holding hands signifies' sentence, choosing the correct meaning of 'standing ovation', and explaining the final line in their own words. Pairs cross-check answers, then teacher leads whole-class verification, drawing out the idea that the last line claims the athletes' act surpasses verbal description.

Students turn to Vocabulary in Context (p.162): working individually to identify two adjective–noun collocations from the poem besides 'standing ovation'. Teacher models the concept using the example, then asks students to share and justify their choices, noting how the adjective sharpens or intensifies the noun it accompanies.

A quick paired exchange consolidates the collocation concept: each pair brainstorms one further adjective–noun pair from their own knowledge that fits the poem's emotional register, then shares with the class. Teacher notes two or three examples on the board as a springboard for the fuller collocation table task that follows in the vocabulary unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Having analysed imagery and tone in the preceding work on the poem, students are now ready to read a specific extract with evaluative precision — asking why the poet ended where she did and what the final line claims. A frequent misread of the last line is that it is self-deprecating; guide students toward the interpretation that it celebrates the athletes' act as beyond language. The fuller collocation table task (p.162) and the adjective-replacement sentences (p.163) are assigned to the vocabulary unit that follows, not here.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary in Context (p.162): complete the collocation table — four nouns each for heavy, strong, large, great
Vocabulary in Context (p.163): choose the correct adjective from the box for five underlined words in sentences

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the adjective–noun collocation concept using 'standing ovation' and the two examples students found in the poem during the previous work. The class is then introduced to the collocation table task (p.162), with the completed row for 'big' as a shared model before students proceed.

Students complete the collocation table (p.162) individually, writing four nouns each for 'heavy', 'strong', 'large', and 'great'. Pairs compare answers and note where they agree or differ; teacher facilitates a brief class discussion on why some collocations sound natural while others sound odd, drawing on the poem's own language where relevant.

Students work through the five adjective-replacement sentences (p.163), selecting the correct adjective from the given box for each underlined word and ensuring no adjective is used twice. Teacher draws attention to the semantic range each adjective covers and how the poem's own descriptions of the athletes informed the choice of words in each sentence.

Class shares answers aloud; teacher corrects and briefly explains any contested choice. Students write one original sentence using any collocation from the table, using it to describe an athlete or moment from the poem — this bridges the vocabulary work back to the text.

periods.teacher_notes: Vocabulary/Grammar occupies its own unit here as required; the collocation table and adjective-replacement tasks are best done together since both draw on context-sensitive adjective choice, and the poem provides a natural anchor. Students often conflate 'large' and 'great' collocations — a brief class discussion of why 'a great crowd' sounds more natural than 'a large spirit' is valuable here. No tasks from this spine remain unanchored.

periods.activity_title: Patrick Gomes Radio-Talk and Special Olympics Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.163): listen to radio-talk on Patrick Gomes; write true or false for three statements
Listen and Respond (p.164): listen again; choose the correct option for five questions
Speaking Activity (p.164): paired discussion on Special Olympics — importance, impact, awareness — using sentence starters

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly contextualises the radio-talk: Patrick Gomes is a special athlete and coach whose story extends the poem's theme of limitless possibility into a real life. Students are told to listen for key facts about his career path and beliefs.

Teacher reads the transcript (p.268) aloud at a natural pace while students listen and write 'true' or 'false' for the three statements (p.163). After a brief pause, teacher reads the transcript a second time and students answer the five multiple-choice questions (p.164), then pairs compare answers before teacher verifies.

Teacher leads a whole-class check of both listening tasks, clarifying why Patrick Gomes's participation at the Connecticut Special Olympics was a turning point and what his current role as a coach involves. Any misconceptions surfaced by the multiple-choice answers are addressed here.

Students move into pairs for the Speaking Activity (p.164): taking turns to share views on Special Olympics — its importance as a vehicle for inclusion, its impact on athletes with special abilities, and ways to create awareness. They use the provided sentence starters and are encouraged to agree or disagree with their partner's points with reasons, modelling a focused dialogue.

Three or four pairs share one exchange with the class; teacher notes the most persuasive uses of the sentence starters on the board. Students are asked to reflect briefly in writing on one idea from the discussion that they found most compelling, connecting it back to the poem's closing image of nine beaming faces.

periods.teacher_notes: The radio-talk about Patrick Gomes directly extends the poem's theme of empathy and collective humanity into a real-world context, so the transition from poem to transcript should be made explicit. Students may struggle with the distinction between Patrick Gomes's current role as coach and his earlier career as a special athlete — the MCQ on his present status is a reliable diagnostic. The paired speaking task works best when the sentence starters are visible; write three examples on the board before pairs begin.

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic devices, tone, imagery, and thematic meaning using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Nine Special Olympics athletes choosing collective solidarity over individual victory in a hundred-yard dash.
items.item_stem:
Read the stanza on p.157, beginning "The signal was given, the pistol exploded". Which of the following best describes the effect of the phrase "the pistol exploded" on the reader?
A. It suggests the starting pistol was faulty and dangerous.
B. It creates a vivid auditory image that conveys the sudden, violent start of the race.
C. It implies the athletes were startled and unprepared for the race.
D. It shows that the race official was careless with the equipment.

options.label: A
options.text: It creates a vivid auditory image that conveys the sudden, violent start of the race.

options.label: B
options.text: It implies the athletes were startled and unprepared for the race.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows that the race official was careless with the equipment.

options.label: D
options.text: It suggests the starting pistol was faulty and dangerous.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student reads 'exploded' literally rather than as an auditory image signalling the race's explosive start.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student confuses the effect on the runners with the effect on the reader, missing the auditory imagery function.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student interprets the word at face value without attending to its figurative and sensory role in the poem.

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic devices, tone, imagery, and thematic meaning using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Nine Special Olympics athletes choosing collective solidarity over individual victory in a hundred-yard dash.
items.item_stem:
Read the second stanza on p.157, beginning "The eight other runners pulled up on their heels".

1. What does the phrase "pulled up on their heels" tell us about what the eight runners did, and why is it significant at this moment in the poem?
2. The poet writes that the runners went back "one by one". What does this detail suggest about the nature of their decision to help?
3. How does the tone of this stanza differ from the tone of the stanza immediately before it, and what poetic effect does that shift create?
items.visual_stimulus: Read the second stanza on p.157, beginning "The eight other runners pulled up on their heels".

expected_elements: Identifies 'pulled up on their heels' as meaning the runners stopped mid-race.
Notes the significance: trained competitors sacrificed their chance at a medal.
Explains 'one by one' as showing the decision spread voluntarily, not as a group command.
Contrasts the preceding stanza's anguish with this stanza's quiet resolve or compassion.
Names the tonal shift as moving from individual distress to collective solidarity.

items.source_lo: Student demonstrates focused listening comprehension by verifying factual statements and selecting correct information from an oral text.
items.source_context: Radio-talk about Patrick Gomes, a special athlete turned coach who began his career in 1991.
items.item_stem:
Your teacher will read the radio-talk about Patrick Gomes aloud. Listen carefully and write TRUE or FALSE for each statement below.
(1) Patrick Gomes first participated in track events in Chennai in 1991.
(2) Patrick Gomes was selected for his first Special Olympics World Summer Games while studying at Okhla Centre of Learning and Development.
(3) Patrick Gomes has been coaching special athletes for more than twenty years.

options.text: Patrick Gomes first participated in track events in Chennai in 1991.
Patrick Gomes has been coaching special athletes for more than twenty years.
Patrick Gomes was selected for his first Special Olympics World Summer Games while studying at Okhla Centre of Learning and Development.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (1) TRUE — the transcript states his journey began with track events in Chennai in 1991. (2) TRUE — the transcript confirms he was selected while a student at Okhla Centre of Learning and Development. (3) FALSE — the transcript states he has been coaching special athletes for over 15 years, not more than twenty.

items.source_lo: Student demonstrates focused listening comprehension by verifying factual statements and selecting correct information from an oral text.
items.source_context: Radio-talk about Patrick Gomes, a special athlete turned coach who began his career in 1991.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the radio-talk about Patrick Gomes a second time. Then answer the following questions in one or two sentences each.
(1) The radio speaker says Patrick Gomes participates in his sport despite having a 'speech challenge'. What does the transcript tell us about how he manages daily life, and what does this reveal about his character?
(2) Patrick Gomes believes sports is important for everyone. According to the radio-talk, what three qualities does he say sports develops? Why might these qualities be especially significant for a special athlete?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (1) The transcript says Patrick Gomes lives by himself and does all daily household chores independently despite his speech challenge, revealing that he is a confident and self-reliant person. (2) He says sports develops positivity, fitness, and discipline; for a special athlete these qualities are especially significant because they build independence and resilience in the face of additional challenges.

items.source_lo: Student expresses and defends a reasoned point of view in a structured paired discussion using a poem's theme as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Paired discussion on the importance, impact, and awareness of Special Olympics and inclusion in sport.
items.item_stem: In pairs, take turns sharing your views on the following statement: 'Inclusion in sport matters more than winning medals.' One partner argues in favour of this view; the other raises a counter-point with reasons. Draw on what you know about the Special Olympics and the events described in 'Nine Gold Medals' to support your position. Use phrases such as 'Personally, I believe that…' and 'I would like to add that…' to structure your turns.

expected_elements: States a clear personal position on inclusion versus winning at the outset.
Supports the view with a specific reference to the poem's events or theme.
Acknowledges and responds to the partner's counter-point with a reason.
Uses at least one structured sentence starter appropriately.
Speaks with sufficient clarity and coherence to sustain a two-turn exchange.

items.source_lo: Student expresses and defends a reasoned point of view in a structured paired discussion using a poem's theme as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Paired discussion on the importance, impact, and awareness of Special Olympics and inclusion in sport.
items.item_stem: Your teacher will read a short scenario aloud: 'A local newspaper has reported that a school sports day is considering dropping its inclusive relay race — where students with and without disabilities run together — to save time. Parents are divided.' Hold a brief open-house dialogue with two or three classmates. One group argues for keeping the inclusive race; the other argues for removing it. Each speaker must give at least one reason and respond to at least one point made by the other side. You may refer to the spirit of the Special Olympics and the ideas in 'Nine Gold Medals' to strengthen your argument.

expected_elements: Presents a clearly reasoned argument for or against the inclusive race.
Connects the argument to the poem's theme of collective humanity or solidarity.
Directly engages with and responds to an opposing point raised by a classmate.
Uses appropriate register and turn-taking in the dialogue.
Moves beyond recounting facts to evaluating the value of inclusion in sport.

items.source_lo: Student produces purposeful functional and creative writing using a poem's theme as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Writing slogans and a poster that champion inclusion and human potential in competitive sport.
items.item_stem: Your school's Sports Committee is organising a day of inclusive athletics for students with and without disabilities. Write a notice (80–100 words) for the school notice board announcing the event. Include the name of the event, its purpose, the date and venue (you may invent these details), and a call for student volunteers to assist on the day.

expected_elements: Uses correct notice format: heading, date, body, and issuing authority.
States the event's purpose clearly, connecting to inclusion or empathy.
Includes invented but plausible logistical details (event name, venue, date).
Contains a clear call for volunteer participation.
Stays within the word limit and uses formal, clear language throughout.

items.source_lo: Student produces purposeful functional and creative writing using a poem's theme as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Writing slogans and a poster that champion inclusion and human potential in competitive sport.
items.item_stem: A sports magazine has invited readers to send in a letter to the editor (120–150 words) responding to this comment by a reader: 'Giving every athlete the same medal regardless of finishing position devalues competitive sport.' Write your letter agreeing or disagreeing with this view. Use evidence from the events described in 'Nine Gold Medals' and your own reasoning to support your argument. Sign your letter as 'A Concerned Reader'.

expected_elements: Uses correct letter-to-editor format: salutation, body paragraphs, sign-off.
States a clear position (agree or disagree) in the opening paragraph.
Cites a specific event from the poem as evidence for the argument.
Evaluates the meaning of 'winning' beyond finishing position, with a reasoned claim.
Maintains formal register and stays within the word count.

items.source_lo: Student identifies and applies adjective–noun collocations in context using a poem's vocabulary as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Adjective–noun collocations drawn from and inspired by the language of the poem, including 'standing ovation'.
items.item_stem: The poem uses the collocation 'beaming faces' to describe the athletes at the finish line. In two sentences, explain what the adjective 'beaming' adds to the noun 'faces' that a more neutral adjective such as 'happy' would not, and then write one original sentence using a different adjective–noun collocation from the poem's world of sport and solidarity.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 'Beaming' is more intense and physical than 'happy' — it suggests a radiant, outward glow of emotion visible to the whole crowd, not just an internal feeling. 'Happy faces' would be bland and static, whereas 'beaming faces' captures the athletes' joy as something luminous and expressive. An original example: 'The young runner gave a loud cry of triumph as she crossed the finish line.'

items.source_lo: Student conducts independent research and creates a visual presentation on a cultural or sporting topic using a poem's themes as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Research on Indian Special Olympics achievers and infographic creation on any sport, inspired by the poem.
items.item_stem: Using any available resources, find out about two Indian athletes who have won medals at any Special Olympics World Games. For each athlete, note down the sport, the year, and the medal won. Then, in three to four sentences, explain what their achievements suggest about the importance of the Special Olympics as a platform — drawing a connection to the spirit shown by the nine athletes in David Roth's poem.

expected_elements: Names two Indian athletes with their sport, year, and medal correctly cited.
Explains what their achievements reveal about Special Olympics as a platform for inclusion.
Draws a specific connection to the poem's theme of solidarity or collective humanity.
Uses own words and shows genuine reflection beyond listing facts.
Writes in coherent sentences with appropriate formal register.

items.source_lo: Student conducts independent research and creates a visual presentation on a cultural or sporting topic using a poem's themes as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Research on Indian Special Olympics achievers and infographic creation on any sport, inspired by the poem.
items.item_stem: Design an infographic on the Special Olympics — its history, purpose, and significance for athletes with intellectual disabilities. Your infographic must include: (a) a brief timeline of at least three key milestones in the history of the Special Olympics; (b) one or two statistics about participation (you may use approximate figures from any credible source); (c) a short original slogan (no more than ten words) that captures the spirit of the poem 'Nine Gold Medals'; and (d) at least one illustration or simple diagram. Present your infographic to the class and be ready to explain your choice of slogan.

expected_elements: Timeline includes at least three accurate and clearly labelled milestones.
Statistics are cited with an approximate source or labelled as estimated.
Slogan is original, within ten words, and thematically linked to the poem.
Infographic layout is clear and readable, with at least one illustration or diagram.
Oral presentation explains the slogan's connection to the poem's theme of solidarity.
